title: Why Updates Matter
objective: After this level you can explain why all complex software has security holes, what a zero-day is, and why installing updates quickly matters.
summary: All software has holes, some unknown even to its maker (zero-days). Patches close them, but attackers target unpatched machines for years, as WannaCry showed in 2017.

cards.headline: The fix was out two months before the attack.
cards.body: On May 12, 2017, the WannaCry ransomware began hitting computers, including machines at dozens of NHS trusts in England. The strange part: Microsoft had released a fix for the flaw it used back in March. Why do fixes come before attacks, and why doesn't everyone install them?

cards.headline: Every big program has holes
cards.body: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre puts it bluntly: all systems contain vulnerabilities, flaws an attacker could use. Some are known to the maker. Others nobody has found yet, or only an attacker has. An attack on one of those is called a zero-day, and the name tells the story: the maker has had zero days to fix it.

cards.headline: The race after a patch
cards.body: Once a maker learns of a flaw, it ships a patch: an update that fixes it. Your machine is safe from that flaw only after the patch is installed, and not everyone installs it. CISA, the US cyber defense agency, warns that attackers go after known holes for months or even years after the fix is out.

cards.headline: WannaCry: the gap in action
cards.body: Microsoft fixed the flaw WannaCry used on March 14, 2017. WannaCry arrived on May 12 and hit computers that had not applied the fix. In England, at least 81 of 236 NHS trusts were affected, and the infected organisations were running unpatched or unsupported Windows. So CISA's advice is simple: install updates as soon as possible, and turn on automatic updates so you don't have to remember.

cards.headline: Holes: patched
learned: All systems contain vulnerabilities, some unknown to their makers
A zero-day is a flaw the maker has had zero days to fix
Attackers target known holes for months or years after a patch
WannaCry (2017) hit machines that skipped a two-month-old fix

questions.prompt: What makes a software attack a "zero-day" attack?

options.label: It is launched on the first day a program goes on sale
options.rationale: The name is about the fix, not the sales date.

options.label: It does no damage until a day has passed
options.rationale: Zero-day is about how long the maker has had to fix the flaw.

options.label: It uses a flaw the maker did not yet know about
It only works on computers set to the wrong date
options.rationale: It has nothing to do with the clock.

questions.explanation: A zero-day attack exploits a previously unknown flaw, so the maker has had zero days to fix it.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the race to fix a software flaw in order.
items: A maker learns of a flaw
questions.explanation: Once a maker learns of a flaw, it ships a patch, and your machine is safe from that flaw only after the patch is installed.

questions.prompt: A processor's switches have no idea what they are doing; they simply follow software. Why does that make a flaw in the software matter?

options.label: The switches spot bad instructions and refuse them
options.rationale: The switches have no idea what the data means; software does the telling.

options.label: Flaws only matter in hardware, never in software
options.rationale: All systems, software included, contain vulnerabilities.

options.label: A software flaw fixes itself when the switches restart
options.rationale: Flaws stay until a patch fixes them.

options.label: The hardware carries out the software, flaws and all

questions.explanation: Hardware does the work and software gives the orders, so a flaw in the orders is a flaw an attacker can use.
